title: The Rock That Was Given a Job — Promiscuous Teleology, Speeded Scientist Judgments, Aristotle's Rain Argument & Odds vs. Risk Ratios

teenKit.tldr: Even elite scientists from places like MIT default to seeing conscious purpose in nature when forced to answer questions under tight time pressure. Our brains are hardwired to spot intent everywhere, a cognitive quirk scientists call promiscuous teleology.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding this default setting helps us catch our own biases, showing us why humans so easily confuse random natural events with grand cosmic plans.
keyTakeaways: Promiscuous teleology is our brain's automatic tendency to assign a purpose or design to non-living things, like viewing a rock as a built-in doorstop.
When elite physicists and chemists are stripped of time to deliberate, their deep evolutionary instincts override their scientific training, leading them to endorse intentional design.
Aristotle's classical arguments for nature working toward specific goals still mirror how our untrained, everyday human intuition naturally processes the world.

vocab.meaning: The brain's overactive habit of assuming everything in the universe was designed with a specific purpose or goal in mind.
The mental fork in the road where you must choose between a purely physical explanation and a purposeful design explanation.
An experimental technique where subjects are rushed to answer questions instantly, cutting off their ability to second-guess themselves.
A statistical comparison that helps researchers figure out the actual probability of an event happening under different conditions.

quiz.question: What happens when top-tier physical scientists are forced to answer fundamental physics questions in just three seconds?
options: They give up entirely out of frustration.
They answer with flawless mathematical precision.
They frequently fall back on seeing conscious design and purpose in the universe.
They instantly cite Aristotle's exact historical texts.
quiz.explanation: Tight time pressure disables slow deliberation, revealing our brain's underlying, automatic bias toward intentional design.

quiz.question: When looking at a smooth wedge-shaped stone holding a door open, what does the cognitive crossroads represent?
options: The choice between measuring its physical weight versus calculating its velocity.
The mental split between seeing the stone as a product of mindless erosion versus a purposeful tool.
The debate over whether wooden doors are better than metal ones.
The legal dispute over who placed the rock on the path.
quiz.explanation: It highlights the two competing paths our minds travel: mechanical physical processes versus deliberate, purposeful creation.

quiz.question: Which of the following best defines 'promiscuous teleology'?
options: A biological mutation found only in certain mammals.
An advanced mathematical formula used by MIT physicists.
The default human mental reflex to see intent and purpose everywhere in nature.
A historical theory of gravity introduced by Aristotle.
quiz.explanation: It describes our brain's hyperactive tendency to look at random or physical phenomena and automatically assign them a job or goal.
